parts.label: Part 4
parts.article:
Good morning everyone. In this module we've been looking at various field survey methods, and now I'm going to give you a brief introduction to the specific organism that we'll be focusing on during our first field trip, and that's the gastropod. Gastropods are invertebrates, that is, organisms without a backbone, and they're more commonly known as snails, or if they haven't got a shell, slugs.
Now, in terms of their evolution, gastropods go back a long way. As with other primitive animals, the minerals in their body fluids are very similar to the mineral composition of the sea, indicating that they began life there. And their fossilised remains have been found in rocks dating back at least 500 million years.
Looking at the physical features of the gastropods, well they all have one muscular foot for swimming or walking. This foot is lubricated with mucus, and it's this that leaves the sticky trail that you see behind snails and slugs. They also have an organ called a radula, which they use for feeding. Then of course the snails, though not the slugs, have a shell.
In terms of their dimensions, snail shells in Britain range from the dwarf snail which is 1.5mm long, to the Roman snail, whose shell can be as big as 50mm. As well as size variations, you get a lot of differences in the form of snail shells. For example, the majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left. Then some shells, for instance, the plaited snail, have regularly spaced ribs, while the prickly snail has prominent spines. There are even a number of species with hair on their shells. Colors on the shells also vary as do patterns, so appearances are really varied.
Okay, let's turn now to feeding habits. Most of you who are gardeners will know to your cost that some gastropods eat healthy plants, but you may not realise that these are the minority. Most species feed on rotting plants, or they eat fungi and algae. Some species eat dead animals, and there are some that are actually carnivorous - they prey on live animals. For example, the shield slug feeds on worms.
And apart from their own feeding habits, I should point out that gastropods themselves have plenty of predators. Birds and frogs are the main ones. But there's even an entire family of flies that have specialised in preying on gastropods. And of course, last but not least, I should mention human predators. It was the Romans who probably first introduced edible snails into Britain during the 1st century, and they are still eaten today. In fact, the collection of wild snails for cooking has caused local extinctions of one species, which is also under threat internationally. So there are lots of predators, but to protect themselves, gastropods have often developed special defenses. I'll just give you one example. The glutinous snail avoids predators by folding its mantle over its shell, and turning itself into a very slippery blob of jelly.
Well, turning now to gastropod habitats, most species like dampness and shade. In general, both very hot and very cold weather is bad for gastropods, but dry conditions are the least favourable. Snails cope with this by withdrawing into their shells, and often they form a thick film of mucus over the mouth of their shell to minimise loss of water.
Habitats with a long, stable history tend to support the biggest range of gastropod species. So for instance, long, established forests usually support more species than newer plantations of trees, and old, natural, meadowland is much better than land which has recently been farmed, and there is a small number of highly specialised species that live in unusual habitats. For instance, the blind snail spends its whole life buried under the ground. It's been reported living at depths of two metres, and particularly likes the cavities in old, buried bones apparently, but species like these are exceptional.
But wherever they live, gastropods are often sensitive to pollution, and they don't thrive in areas contaminated by agrochemicals. This means that they are a reliable indication of how healthy our environment is.
Now, at this point I'd like to consider habitat management...

analyses.content: 录音中提到腹足纲动物体液中的矿物质与 sea（海洋）的矿物质成分非常相似，对应题目中的 like those in the...。
As with other primitive animals, the minerals in their body fluids are very similar to the mineral composition of the sea, indicating that they began life there.
听到 minerals 就要警觉，similar to 是题目 like 的同义替换，紧跟其后的名词就是答案。
For example, the majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left.
不要听到后面的 left 就填上去，那是指少数（a few）的情况，题目问的是大多数。
录音指出大多数（majority）蜗牛壳向 right（右）盘旋，对应题目 most shells coil to the...。
Then some shells, for instance, the plaited snail, have regularly spaced ribs, while the prickly snail has prominent spines. There are even a number of species with hair on their shells.
题目是并列结构（ribs, spines or...），听到 Even a number of species with... 就要抓取紧跟其后的名词；注意这里 hair 是不可数/集合名词，不加s。
录音中列举了有些壳上有肋条（ribs）、刺（spines），甚至还有一些物种壳上有 hair（毛发）。
Some species eat dead animals, and there are some that are actually carnivorous - they prey on live animals. For example, the shield slug feeds on worms.
Feeds on 是 eat 的同义替换；注意录音中读的是复数 worms，不要漏掉尾音 's'。
录音举例说盾状蛞蝓以 worms（蠕虫）为食，对应题目 shield slugs eat...。
It was the Romans who probably first introduced edible snails into Britain during the 1st century, and they are still eaten today.
题目空格后没有 "century" 这个词，但在 "in the ___" 的语境下填序数词 1st 或 first 是最符合题意和字数要求的表达。
录音提到罗马人可能是在 1st（第一）世纪将食用蜗牛引入英国的，对应题目 introduced... in the...。
录音说为了保护自己，腹足纲动物通常发展出特殊的 defenses（防御机制），对应题目 particular types of...。
So there are lots of predators, but to protect themselves, gastropods have often developed special defenses. I'll just give you one example.
Special 对应题目中的 particular types of；注意录音中是复数形式，且美式拼写 defenses 或英式 defences 均可。
In general, both very hot and very cold weather is bad for gastropods, but dry conditions are the least favourable.
不要填 hot 或 cold，那是 bad 的条件，题目问的是 worst（最差），对应录音中的最高级 least favourable。
录音提到极热和极冷都不好，但 dry（干燥）条件是最不利的（least favourable），对应题目 ...conditions are worst。
Habitats with a long, stable history tend to support the biggest range of gastropod species. So for instance, long, established forests usually support more species than newer plantations of trees...
不要填 plantations，录音是用它做反面教材（newer plantations 支持的物种较少）；注意 forests 是复数。
录音说历史悠久的 forests（森林）通常支持更多物种，对应题目 old, natural habitats, e.g. ...。
For instance, the blind snail spends its whole life buried under the ground. It's been reported living at depths of two metres...
Buried under 对应题目中的 below，紧跟介词后的名词就是答案；不要填 bones，那是它喜欢的具体居住缝隙，不是大环境。
录音提到盲蜗牛一生都埋在 ground（地下/地面）之下，对应题目 lives entirely below the...。
But wherever they live, gastropods are often sensitive to pollution... This means that they are a reliable indication of how healthy our environment is.
How healthy... is 是 quality of 的同义改写；不要填 pollution，那是影响它们生存的因素，不是它们指示的对象。
录音最后说它们是我们的 environment（环境）有多健康的一个可靠指标，对应题目 quality of the...。
